Many English words come from other languages. The etymology, or history, of a word can help you understand its meaning in English. For example, a centipede is a small insect with many legs. The word centipede comes from the Latin word centipeda, which means a hundred feet.

You can often use the etymology of familiar words to help you uncover the meaning of unfamiliar words. For example, journey and sojourn are related English words that come from French. If you know the meaning of journey, then you can guess that a sojourn is related to traveling. Specifically, it refers to a temporary stay by a traveler or guest.

Amanda rushed inside the house, her clothes already wet from the rain.
<u>Direct addresses</u>
Use commas to set off the name of a person being spoken to.

Thank you, Bella, for your help.

Alexander the Great was Macedonian, not Greek.
Tara, unlike Megan, finds chemistry fascinating.

sentences.text: <u>Complex sentences</u>

If a dependent clause is followed by a complete sentence, use a comma after the dependent clause. These dependent clauses usually start with a subordinating conjunction, such as after, although, as, because, before, if, since, unless, until, when, or while.

Use a comma after mild interjections, as well as words like yes, no, well, and however, when they are followed by a complete sentence.

Yes, that sounds great!
<u>Introductory phrases</u>

Use a comma after most introductory phrases—such as participle phrases, infinitive phrases, and long prepositional phrases—when they are followed by a complete sentence. (Commas are not usually necessary after short prepositional phrases of one or two words.)
In just a few weeks, Mr. Chen will be leaving for his trip to France.
Breathing heavily, Maddie sprinted the last few meters of the race.
<u>Absolute phrases</u>
Use commas to set off absolute phrases. An absolute phrase usually consists of a noun followed by a participle phrase, adjective phrase, or other modifier.
Hands shaking, Tony opened the letter and read it aloud.
Amanda rushed inside the house, her clothes already wet from the rain.
<u>Direct addresses</u>
Use commas to set off the name of a person being spoken to.

Thank you, Bella, for your help.
<u>Interrupters</u>
Use commas to set off interrupters, which are words, phrases, or clauses that interrupt the sentence with extra, or parenthetical, information.
You, of course, may have a different opinion.
The new theme park won't open, I'm sorry to say, until next year.
<u>Antithetical phrases</u>
Use commas to set off phrases that use the words not or unlike to qualify adjacent text.
Alexander the Great was Macedonian, not Greek.
Tara, unlike Megan, finds chemistry fascinating.

Use a comma to separate a pair of coordinate adjectives. Coordinate adjectives are adjectives that describe the same noun equally. You can tell that a pair of adjectives are coordinate if the text still sounds okay when the adjective order is changed as well as when and is inserted.
Victor walked carefully down the slick, icy sidewalk.
Victor walked carefully down the icy, slick sidewalk.
Victor walked carefully down the slick and icy sidewalk.
